query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: When a non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm3) is annealed in the 200–600 °C range, its metastable solid solutions partially decompose into stable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. This precipitation locally depletes and reorganizes the matrix composition, altering the composition and stability of the protective oxide/passivation layers, thereby reducing corrosion rates in chloride media while simultaneously enhancing high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or rapidly consolidated Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with retained metastable solid solution and minor intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Post-synthesis annealing at moderate temperatures (200–600 °C) for controlled dwell times, followed by exposure to corrosive (e.g., NaCl) and high-temperature oxidative environments.
generation.conditions: Alloy composition designed with multiple principal elements, total density below 6 g/cm3, Mg as one major constituent, a non-equilibrium microstructure, and subsequent systematic heat treatments in inert or air atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases from the original metastable phase(s), accompanied by changes in the matrix compositions near these precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Intermetallic precipitation rearranges local composition and influences the chemistry of oxide/passivation films, improving their adherence or protective properties under corrosive and oxidative conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the non-annealed baseline, annealed alloys exhibit lower corrosion current densities in chloride solution (indicating better corrosion resistance) and slower mass gain (or scale growth) under high-temperature oxidative environments (≥200 °C).
generation.baseline: The as-cast or non-annealed alloy state with metastable phases will show higher corrosion current densities and accelerated oxide growth at elevated temperature in comparison to the annealed condition.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the alloy maintains non-equilibrium phases prior to annealing, contains sufficient Mg to promote stable precipitated phases, and remains below 6 g/cm3 in density. Significant deviations from these conditions may limit or alter the proposed phase decomposition and passivation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Exact phase fractions, precipitation kinetics, and the extent of local compositional changes at phase interfaces remain insufficiently quantified under varying thermal histories and are subject to ongoing investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two nearly identical alloy batches with the target Mg-containing composition. Retain one batch in the as-cast state and anneal the other in multiple 100 °C increments (200–600 °C) for fixed times. Perform electrochemical corrosion tests in 0.1–0.5 M NaCl solutions and thermogravimetric oxidation measurements up to 600 °C in air.
measurements: Phase fraction and distribution via XRD (in situ if feasible) and SEM/EDS before and after annealing.
Corrosion current densities and open-circuit potentials from potentiodynamic polarization in NaCl.
Mass gain (from TGA) or oxide scale thickness and spallation by ex situ SEM/EDS after isothermal oxidation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealing does not lead to measurable formation of new Mg-rich intermetallic phases or if post-anneal corrosion rates and oxidation behaviors remain unchanged (i.e., no improvement in corrosion resistance or no difference in scaling kinetics versus the as-cast baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,].
